summary: This program keeps a travel packing list in an ArrayList of strings, prints it as a numbered list, then adds one item and removes another by name before printing the list again. It shows that a List allows duplicate values and that removing by name only takes out the first match.

lines.text: ArrayList is the everyday List implementation in Java, and it lives in the java.util package, so it has to be imported before you can use it.
List is the interface that describes what any list can do; importing it lets you declare variables by that general type.

The variable is declared as a List but built as an ArrayList, which is the habit to form: code against the interface so the underlying implementation can change later. The <String> says this list holds only strings.
A List, unlike a Set, happily stores the same value twice, which is exactly what you want when you are packing two pairs of socks.
Counting from 0 up to items.size() - 1 walks every position in the list; size() reports how many items are currently stored.
get(i) pulls out the item at that position, and i + 1 turns the zero-based index into human-friendly numbering that starts at 1.
The \n escape sequence prints a newline first, leaving a blank line so the output sections stay visually separated.
Adding to an ArrayList appends the new item at the end, so Shampoo lands after Socks.
Passing a string to remove deletes the first element equal to it and leaves the second Socks in place; passing an int instead would remove by position.
